title: Who is my mother (Mark 3:20–35)
hookLine: his relatives come; he says whoever does God's will is his family; Catholics read brethren as kin, as Aramaic allows

cards: Someone in a family starts doing something the rest don't understand. Quits the job. Joins something.
Moves away. And the relatives start talking: is he all right? Has she lost it?
Somebody should bring him home. The crowds are so thick he can't even eat. Mark says his own people hear about it and set out to take charge of him, because they're saying he's out of his mind.
Then his mother and brothers arrive, stand outside, and send someone in to call him.

teach.b: Mark tells this as a sandwich: family, an argument, family again. First, the middle. Scribes come down from Jerusalem and say Jesus drives out demons by the power of the devil.
He answers with a picture: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Why would Satan fight Satan? Second, the doorway.

Someone tells him: your mother and your brethren are outside, looking for you. He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is my mother and my brethren?" He looks around at the people sitting in a circle at his feet.

teach.h: BEHOLD MY MOTHER AND MY BRETHREN.
teach.b: "Behold my mother and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother." It can sound cold. It isn't a rejection; it's a widening, open now to anyone who does God's will.

Third, Mary. Catholics notice that no one did God's will more fully than Mary, who said yes to God before Jesus was born. Saint Augustine said she was more blessed for being his disciple than for being his mother.
So this saying doesn't push her out.

teach.h: WHOSOEVER SHALL DO THE WILL OF GOD.
teach.b: Christians read who they are differently.
Catholics believe Mary remained a virgin, and read brethren as relatives, kin, since the Bible can use brother for wider family; in Genesis, Abraham calls his nephew Lot his brother.
Orthodox tradition holds they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. A common Protestant reading takes them as younger children of Mary and Joseph.
Each reads the same verse carefully, and the text itself doesn't settle it.

how: Catholics honor Mary as the first and most faithful disciple, and call one another brothers and sisters in Christ; the Church teaches Mary's perpetual virginity and reads the Lord's brethren as his relatives.

o: servants hired to carry the bags

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: he casts out devils by the devil

s: Jesus rejects his mother in this story
he widens the family to all who do God's will, and Catholics see Mary as its best example.
in Hebrew and Aramaic, brother could mean a cousin or nephew
in Genesis, Abraham calls his nephew Lot his brother.
all Christians read the brethren of Jesus the same way
Catholics read kin, Orthodox tradition reads Joseph's children, and a common Protestant reading is younger siblings.

games.q: you're teaching a packed room, and someone says: your mother and brothers are outside asking for you. what does Jesus do?
o: go out and go home with them.
point at the circle and say: behold my mother and my brethren.
games.why: he looks around at the people at his feet: "Behold my mother and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother."

practice: Think of someone you'll probably pass today without a second look, a cashier, a bus driver, a new kid at school, the neighbor you've never spoken to, and picture their face.

Now picture them sitting in that circle around Jesus, and hear him say: behold my brother, my sister. If you pray, hold them there a while; if you don't, simply wish them well as you would your own family.

wordCard.voice: Brethren. The brothers at the door, and Jesus's answer: whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, my mother. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: brothers, brethren; in Semitic usage the word behind it could cover wider kin.

carryVoice: Your line: family by doing God's will. The circle is wider than the door. Day two hundred, and counting.
